'''Charles Eugène Fabry''' ({{IPA|fr|øʒɛn fabʁi|lang}}; 16 October 1856{{snd}}6 October 1944) was a French [[mathematician]]. Fabry is best known for studying the [[Singularity (mathematics)|singularities]] of [[analytic functions]], including proving the [[Fabry gap theorem]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Fabry|first= Eugène|title=Sur les points singuliers d'une fonction donnée par son développement en série et l'impossibilité du prolongement analytique dans des cas très généraux|journal=Annales scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure |series=Série 3|volume=13|year=1896|pages=367–399|doi=10.24033/asens.431}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Pólya | first = George
 | doi = 10.2307/1990153
 | journal = Transactions of the American Mathematical Society
 | mr = 6577
 | pages = 65–71
 | title = On converse gap theorems
 | volume = 52
 | year = 1942}}</ref>

==Biography==
Eugène Fabry, born in [[Marseille]], was the second of five sons in his family. His brothers included physicist [[Charles Fabry]] and astronomer [[Louis Fabry]].<ref name=charles>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Lecomte | first1 = Jean
 | last2 = Arnulf | first2 = Albert
 | last3 = Vassy | first3 = E.
 | date = June 1973
 | doi = 10.1364/ao.12.001117
 | issue = 6
 | journal = Applied Optics
 | page = 1117
 | title = Charles Fabry
 | volume = 12}}</ref>

He became professor of analysis at [[Aix-Marseille University]] and the [[University of Montpellier]], and a corresponding member of the [[French Academy of Sciences]].<ref name=charles/>

He was the 1930 recipient of the [[Prix Francoeur]] of the French Academy of Sciences, "for his work on the singularities of analytical functions".<ref>{{cite journal
 | date = January 1931
 | doi = 10.1038/127181a0
 | issue = 3196
 | journal = Nature
 | pages = 181–182
 | title = Prize Awards of the Paris Academy of Sciences
 | volume = 127}}</ref>
